transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-03-14 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes (recording)
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Ellen (Verdigris CTO), Priya (Verdigris SRE), Marco (Verdigris ML), Darren (Verdigris Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
Verdigris is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment for a high-throughput streaming agent product with variable token bursts. Main asks: p95 <= 300ms for short replies, sustained token/sec targets during peak bursts, cost/capacity tradeoffs. Customer to share sample traffic and prompts; Redwood to run token/sec/streaming bench and propose Dedicated pilot.

Topics:
- p95 targets and definition
- streaming vs non-streaming workloads and multiplexing
- concurrency, warm vs cold starts, prefix/KV cache behaviour
- quantization / cost tradeoffs and fallback model routing
- security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, data residency

Questions (captured):
- What does Redwood measure for p95 — end-to-end or just server-side?
- How does batching affect tail latency for streaming?
- Can Dedicated match hosting for p95 at given concurrency?

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining on a friday afternoon, i'm Maya from Redwood, with me are Liam and Sofia on the SE side. we heard Verdigris is building that tokenstorm agent product so wanted to understand your p95 and throughput needs.
[00:09] Ellen: yeah thanks, appreciate it. quick intro — i'm ellen, cto. we've got priya on infra and marco on the model side. darren is here for procurement questions.
[00:18] Priya: hi. quick context — prod traffic is spiky, we see silence most of the day and then bursts where a few hundred concurrent sessions each stream 50–300 tokens in like 3–10s. our goal is p95 under 300ms for short replies (under 64 tokens) and p95 under 700–800ms for longer streaming replies, those are soft numbers. cost is a big concern.
[00:35] Marco: to add, our model is a 16B open model, we plan to quantize for inference. we also sometimes fall back to a smaller model for cost control.
[00:44] Liam: cool, thanks. couple clarifying q's — when you say streaming, do you mean server-sent events-style token streaming to clients? and the p95 target is end-to-end client-observed?
[00:52] Ellen: yes SSE streaming. and p95 ideally end-to-end but we can separate network overhead in our metrics; want to know Redwood's server-side p95 too.
[01:00] Sofia: perfect. one note: our hosted API reports are end-to-end (RTT), but for dedicated/private you typically get closer to server-only numbers because of VPC placement.
[01:10] Marco: what about concurrency — what's realistic on dedicated? we expect burst concurrency of ~350 active streams, peak token/sec around 10k during a 30s surge.
[01:18] Liam: nice, that's helpful. to make sure we're aligned: we usually think in terms of issued requests per second and tokens per second on the backend. for a 16B quantized model on A100-equivalent, a single instance's steady streaming throughput will vary with batch settings and kv cache hit rate. can you share your typical session lengths and sample prompts?
[01:34] Ellen: yes we'll export a sample traffic CSV, includes session start timestamps, latency observed, token counts. we'll attach top prompts too.
[01:40] Darren: from procurement, also need pricing bands for hosted vs dedicated with reserved capacity, what's the delta?
[01:46] Maya: good question — we'll send an initial pricing sheet. quick framing: hosted is easiest to start, dedicated gives more predictable throughput and can hit lower per-token costs with reserved capacity, private/VPC adds compliance but higher ops. depending on your SLA needs we can design a Dedicated config for burst absorb.
[02:02] Priya: what's your warmup behavior? cold-starts are killer for us — we care about steady-state tail.
[02:08] Liam: we have a couple levers — auto-warm pools, preforked workers, and prefix/KV cache. for streaming workloads KV cache is huge if you reuse context across requests (e.g., system + few-shot prompts). we also do continuous batching but with latency SLOs so it limits batch windows.
[02:23] Marco: how do batches interact with streaming? won't you buffer tokens and delay streaming until a full batch forms?
[02:29] Sofia: good point. our runtime supports continuous token-by-token emission while still leveraging micro-batches for kernel efficiency. in practice micro-batches are very small for low-latency streams (2–8 requests) and we cap wait windows to keep p95 low.
[02:43] Ellen: any numbers for p95 at various concurrencies? even rough ballpark helps.
[02:48] Liam: we can share model-by-model profiles but rough example: hosted short reply p95 (server only) for a 16B quantized model with streaming enabled — low concurrency (<=20): ~120–180ms, mid (100–200): ~200–350ms, high (300–500): 300–550ms depending on KV hit and batch config. hosted also adds network vlat overhead. Dedicated unit sizing with pinned GPUs often improves tail since you can dedicate capacity and reduce noisy neighbors.
[03:18] Priya: are those numbers measured on A100 or on lower-tier gpus? we use cloud nvidia t4s internally; curious if Redwood has profiles across hardware.
[03:26] Liam: we profile across A100, H100, and Ampere-class inferencing cards; we'll attach a performance matrix. for T4-class, expect ~1.5–2x slower than A100 for heavy attention ops.
[03:35] Marco: what about prefix cache hit rates — what do you need to see a 2x improvement?
[03:40] Sofia: it's use-case dependent; if your requests reuse a sizeable shared prefix we often see 30–70% reduction in per-token compute. we'll want to look at the sample prompts.
[03:49] Ellen: on the security front, SOC2 is required — we saw Redwood's SOC2 mention on the site, can you provide the report and details on KMS and SSO?
[03:57] Maya: absolutely. we'll share the SOC2 pack and the Private deployment notes for KMS/HSM integrations and SAML/SSO options. Dedicated also supports customer-managed keys in many configs.
[04:07] Darren: any data residency guarantees? some of our customers are EU-only.
[04:11] Maya: hosted has region choices and data residency controls; private on-prem or VPC gives you full locality control. we'll include region availability in the follow-ups.
[04:19] Marco: ok practical benchmarking — we want Redwood to run a token/sec and p95 streaming benchmark using our prompt set. what would you need from us to run that?
[04:27] Liam: ideally: 1) sample prompts (top 20–50), 2) traffic CSV of session patterns, 3) target p95 SLOs you'd accept, and 4) preferred models (quantized 16B and a fallback 7B). with that we can simulate bursts and provide a report with p95, p50, tokens/sec, and cost estimate.
[04:40] Marco: we can get that to you by tuesday.
[04:42] Ellen: we also need to know the decision timeline — we want to be in pilot within ~4 weeks if the numbers look good.
[04:48] Maya: that's doable. we recommend a 2-week Dedicated pilot to validate burst absorb. we can do hosted pilot first if you want faster iteration.
[04:55] Priya: is there friction switching between hosted and dedicated later? like does the API change?
[04:58] Maya: one of Redwood's selling points is the unified API — same request shape and rollout controls across environments. config/ops will differ but the app integration is minimal.
[05:07] Marco: edge-case — we sometimes do long-context sessions (1–2k tokens). how does that change tail?
[05:12] Liam: long contexts increase KV and attention costs; tail increases nonlinearly with length. we'd recommend quantization + chunked contexts and prioritizing KV cache hits. also in Dedicated you can pick more memory-heavy instances for long-context workloads.
[05:25] Ellen: what's the failover story — if a Dedicated pool is saturated can Redwood route to hosted fallback?
[05:30] Sofia: yes, smart routing supports fallback to hosted or to a smaller model variant; you can configure cost-first or latency-first policies.
[05:38] Darren: procurement question — SLAs on p95? can Redwood commit to 300ms p95?
[05:43] Maya: SLAs are tied to the deployment mode and our operational guarantees; 300ms p95 for end-to-end streaming is tough for many public cloud setups at high concurrency — but server-side p95 under 300ms for short replies is achievable with Dedicated and the right hardware. we should confirm with real benchmarks.
[05:58] Marco: any recommendations for initial Dedicated sizing? we need to absorb 10k tokens/sec peaks and 350 concurrent streams.
[06:05] Liam: preliminary thumb rule — for a 16B quantized model on high-density inference hardware, that workload maps to roughly 6–8 GPUs with aggressive KV caching and preforking, but that depends on exact token length distribution and reuse. we'll propose 2 sizing options: cost-optimized and latency-optimized.
[06:20] Priya: can Redwood run a quick internal sim so we have a cost-ballpark?
[06:24] Maya: yes we'll run a sim once you share the CSV.
[06:27] Ellen: do you support end-to-end tracing to attribute latency to network vs compute? we need that for observability.
[06:32] Sofia: we emit per-request traces, token-level timing and model stage breakdowns in the Console. those can be shipped to your tracing backend.
[06:41] Marco: for the benchmark, will you run both hosted and dedicated and show variance?
[06:45] Liam: yes we can run both, and also a quantized vs non-quantized comparison. we'll include streaming p95 plots and token/sec heatmaps.
[06:53] Ellen: what's typical quantization impact on p95?
[06:56] Liam: quantization reduces memory and often speeds up kernel calls by 20–40% depending on model and hardware — we have profiles in our performance matrix. sometimes tail variability increases slightly on smaller hardware.
[07:08] Darren: procurement: we need a basic SOW for a pilot: timeline, acceptance criteria, exit criteria, and cost. can you provide that?
[07:15] Maya: yes we'll draft a simple SOW for a 2-week Dedicated pilot: objectives (validate p95 and burst absorb), acceptance (p95 under X ms for Y% of traffic), and next steps.
[07:23] Priya: what are common gotchas you've seen during pilots?
[07:26] Sofia: most common: 1) mismatch in sample workload vs prod (underspecing bursts), 2) not instrumenting end-to-end metrics properly, 3) forgetting to factor network/regional egress. we try to catch these in the kick-off.
[07:38] Marco: ok let's narrow down follow-ups — i'll send sample prompts + traffic CSV by tuesday; can you commit to running hosted and dedicated bench within 5 business days of that?
[07:48] Liam: yes we can aim for 5 business days, depends on queue but we'll queue it as high priority for this pilot.
[07:55] Ellen: timeline wise — if benchmarks look good we want pilot start ~4/1.
[07:59] Maya: sounds good.
[08:02] [brief pause]
[08:05] (small crosstalk)
[08:09] Ellen: one more — do you have an example dashboard showing p95 over time and token/sec correlation?
[08:13] Sofia: yes, we'll include dashboard screenshots and sample traces in the follow-up.
[08:18] Darren: any discount structure for pilots?
[08:21] Maya: we typically offer pilot credits and price protection during pilot-to-production transition if you commit to Dedicated. details in the SOW.
[08:29] Marco: last technical: how do you handle KV cache eviction during spikes? could eviction cause tail spikes?
[08:34] Liam: eviction can increase latency for those requests that miss the cache; we do predictive warming and LRU with priority for sessions in-flight. in Dedicated you can tune cache size to reduce eviction risk.
[08:47] Priya: okay good. any blockers on our side?
[08:50] Ellen: none; procurement will need SOW and initial pricing to sign off.
[08:55] Maya: recap and next steps: 1) Verdigris sends sample prompts and traffic CSV (Marco/Ellen) by 2026-03-17; 2) Redwood (Maya/Liam) sends benchmark plan, pricing bands, SOC2/security pack and proposed Dedicated configs by 3/18; 3) schedule cluster sizing workshop week of 3/22; 4) target pilot start 4/1.
[09:15] Darren: sounds good.
[09:18] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the assets and SOW.
[09:22] Ellen: thanks, talk soon.
